name: Serial memory processing
statement: The time to judge whether a probe was in a memorised set rises by about 38 milliseconds per item, which Sternberg read as a serial search through memory.
meaning: This names a claim about how memory is searched, not a claim that anybody judges anything wrongly. Sternberg's task shows a person a short series of digits, waits about two seconds, then shows one test digit. The person pulls one lever if the digit was in the series and the other lever if it was not. Mean reaction time rises in a straight line with the number of items held. Sternberg read that straight line as the trace of a serial comparison process, the probe checked against each stored item in turn at a rate no introspection reports. The slopes for present and absent probes came out equal, and he read that as showing the search runs to the end of the list even after a match is found. A search that stopped at the match would need, on average, half as many comparisons on present trials, and so half the slope. Neither half of this describes an error, a norm, or a shortfall against one. The phrase covers the architecture claim and also the primacy and recency effects measured in the same task, and this entry is about the architecture claim. The recall pattern is treated separately under the recency effect, entry 90.

origin.note: The two-page report in volume 153, issue 3736, pages 652 to 654, is where the paradigm and the serial-exhaustive reading were set out. Sternberg does not use the phrase serial memory processing, and it appears in none of the four papers read for this entry. His own terms are serial-comparison process and exhaustive scanning, and his 2016 review calls the mechanism serial exhaustive search.

evidence: Experiment 1 showed eight subjects a random series of one to six different digits, each displayed for 1.2 seconds, followed by a 2.0-second delay, a warning signal and the test digit. Linear regression accounted for 99.4 percent of the variance in the overall mean latencies, with about 95 observations behind each point. The fitted slope was 37.9 plus or minus 3.8 milliseconds per symbol and the zero intercept 397.2 plus or minus 19.3 milliseconds. Lines fitted separately to positive and negative responses differed in slope by 9.6 plus or minus 2.3 milliseconds per symbol, and Sternberg attributed almost all of that to set size one, where positive responses ran 50.0 plus or minus 20.1 milliseconds faster. Across set sizes two to six the slope difference was 3.1 plus or minus 3.2 milliseconds per symbol, which he called insignificant. Experiment 2 fixed the positive set for 120 test trials at a time and held both stimulus and response entropy constant while set size varied. Six subjects gave a slope of 38.3 plus or minus 6.1 milliseconds per symbol and an intercept of 369.4 plus or minus 10.1 milliseconds, again with linear regression accounting for 99.4 percent of the variance in the overall means. They pulled the wrong lever on 1.0 percent of test trials. Sternberg put the implied scanning rate at between 25 and 30 symbols per second, about four times the fastest rate of subvocal speech for digit names, and concluded that the silent rehearsal his subjects reported maintains the memory rather than doing the scanning. He also noted that a self-terminating search could be the inefficient option, if deciding whether a match had occurred were slow and could not run alongside the scan.

replication.headline: Donkin and Nosofsky fitted the three rival architectures to full reaction-time distributions and the serial exhaustive model lost heavily under fast presentation and drew level under slow presentation, so the architecture the linear function is supposed to reveal depends on how the list was shown.
replication.detail: Donkin and Nosofsky formalised serial exhaustive, parallel self-terminating and global access architectures, ran each item comparison as a linear ballistic accumulator, and ranked 36 models by Bayesian information criterion for each participant separately. The fast-rate data came from the four participants in Nosofsky, Little, Donkin and Fific's second experiment, each with about 5,000 trials and study items shown for 500 milliseconds. Measured against the best model for each participant, the best serial exhaustive model scored 146, 124, 689 and 518 on delta BIC. Letting its encoding time vary with the lag between study and probe brought those to 117, 85, 645 and 353, still far behind. Its named failure was predicting a leading edge of the target distributions that was too fast at small set sizes, while underpredicting the growth of positive skew. The authors then rebuilt Sternberg's own conditions. Three participants completed ten one-hour sessions of 300 trials, with each study item shown for 1,000 milliseconds, a 2,000-millisecond wait before the probe, and ordered recall of the whole list after the recognition response. Set sizes ran from one to five and yielded an average of at least 60 observations in each combination of serial position and set size. There the serial exhaustive model scored 10, 0 and 80 on delta BIC, against 11, 64 and 46 for global familiarity and 0, 88 and 0 for parallel self-terminating. Serial position effects, pronounced under fast presentation, were nearly flat under slow presentation. The authors set out two readings, one architecture whose parameters shift with presentation rate, or a real switch to serial exhaustive search when presentation slows, and endorse neither. Townsend and Fific had found the same split inside one experiment. Five paid participants in Belgrade judged whether a target pseudoword was in a two-item set, over 44 blocks of 128 trials, with errors averaging 0.81 percent. Reading each person's survivor interaction contrast alongside the mean interaction contrast, one participant was serial at both interstimulus intervals, one was parallel at both, and three shifted from serial at 700 milliseconds to parallel at 2,000 milliseconds. The authors point out that averaging those five would have produced additivity and a verdict of seriality for everybody.

study.cite: Donkin, C., & Nosofsky, R. M. (2012). The structure of short-term memory scanning: An investigation using response time distribution models. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 19(3), 363-394.

limits: No effect size appears above because none of the papers read here reports one. They report slopes in milliseconds per item, differences in Bayesian information criterion, and interaction contrasts, so the structured effect-size fields are left empty. Sample sizes are small on purpose. This literature runs a handful of people through thousands of trials each and models them one at a time, which is the right design for reaction-time distributions and the wrong one for estimating how common an architecture is in a population. Sternberg's 2016 review answers the critics on procedural grounds. He separates six tasks of memory interrogation, defines abbreviations for 23 experiments, and argues that the results depend on details of procedure whose importance has not been appreciated. On his account the challenges came from variants rather than from his own varied-set and fixed-set tasks, and the two predictions most often said to be violated, about how reaction-time variance and the shortest reaction time change with set size, rest on assumptions outside his model and are not violated in either of his tasks. He concedes ground of his own. Section 11 of that paper says there is little evidence to decide whether the model describes serial comparison or merely serial activation, and his conclusion says many questions remain about how people decide whether an item is in active memory. McElree and Dosher, whose speed-accuracy work is the study most often cited against serial scanning, is paywalled and was not read; what appears here about it is Sternberg's description and a sentence Henson, Hartley, Burgess, Hitch and Flude wrote, which Sternberg quotes. Hockley's reaction-time distribution analysis is paywalled and reaches this page only through Donkin and Nosofsky, who report matching his growth in the skew parameter with set size but a much larger growth in the leading edge than he found. Searches covered Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, Unpaywall and web search, and located no meta-analysis of memory-scanning architecture.
misreadings: Filing this as a bias is the first error, and it is a filing error rather than a reading of the evidence. Sternberg's subjects were right on 99 percent of trials, and the finding is about how long a correct answer took. Nothing in the paradigm identifies a judgement, a normative standard, or a gap between them. The phrase reaches bias lists through Wikipedia, whose article on serial memory processing carries the tag Category:Memory biases, a category whose own page places it inside Category:Cognitive biases. Wikipedia's List of cognitive biases does not contain it. What that list carries from this territory is the serial position effect, with primacy, recency and the suffix effect underneath it, and those are patterns in what gets recalled rather than claims about how a search runs. The second error is treating the straight line as proof of seriality. Townsend and Fific state the mimicry problem plainly: models of either kind can be prescribed to imitate the opposite kind, which is why they built a distribution-free factorial test instead of reading slopes. Their test then found seriality in some people and parallelism in others. The third error is quoting the exhaustive conclusion as settled. It is the part of Sternberg's inference that rests on a null result, the near-equality of two slopes, and it is what the modelling literature has moved furthest from. Baddeley called for a moratorium on reading these measures as direct indices of mental processes, Dosher and Sperling called the model incorrect, and Jonides and colleagues wrote that serial-scanning models fell out of favour; all three are quoted here from Sternberg's own review, which reproduces them before answering them. The fourth error is smaller and travels with the Wikipedia article, which cites the 1966 paper as Science, volume 153, issue 1. Crossref gives issue 3736, pages 652 to 654.

sources.text: Sternberg, S. (1966). High-speed scanning in human memory. Science, 153(3736), 652-654. Read in full from the scan on the author's University of Pennsylvania page; the source of every slope, intercept, subject count and error rate above.

Sternberg, S. (2016). In defence of high-speed memory scanning. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 69(10), 2020-2075. Read from the author's own copy, for the six tasks, the 23 experiments, the section 11 concession, and the quotations from critics reproduced in its section 1.1.

Donkin, C., & Nosofsky, R. M. (2012). The structure of short-term memory scanning: An investigation using response time distribution models. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 19(3), 363-394. Read in full from the publisher's open PDF, for the delta BIC tables, the two experiments and the authors' two readings of them.

Townsend, J. T., & Fific, M. (2004). Parallel versus serial processing and individual differences in high-speed search in human memory. Perception & Psychophysics, 66(6), 953-962. Read in full from the publisher's open PDF, for the five participants, the error rate and the per-person serial and parallel verdicts.

Nosofsky, R. M., Little, D. R., Donkin, C., & Fific, M. (2011). Short-term memory scanning viewed as exemplar-based categorization. Psychological Review, 118(2), 280-315. Abstract read through the Europe PMC REST service, linked here. The data from its second experiment reach this page through Donkin and Nosofsky's refitting of them.

Townsend, J. T. (1990). Serial vs. parallel processing: Sometimes they look like Tweedledum and Tweedledee but they can (and should) be distinguished. Psychological Science, 1(1), 46-54. Named as the source of the mimicry argument on the strength of Townsend and Fific's description; the record was verified at Crossref and the paper was not read.

McElree, B., & Dosher, B. A. (1989). Serial position and set size in short-term memory: The time course of recognition. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 118(4), 346-373. Paywalled and closed at Unpaywall; the record was verified at Crossref and the paper is described here only as Sternberg's review describes it.

Hockley, W. E. (1984). Analysis of response time distributions in the study of cognitive processes. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 10(4), 598-615. Paywalled and closed at Unpaywall; the record was verified at Crossref and the comparison of its ex-Gaussian parameters is read from Donkin and Nosofsky.
